title: Present Perfect Tense
description: Learn the Present Perfect Tense (has/have + V3): form, uses, time markers (just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for), common errors, practice exercises and tests. Bilingual notes.

topics.title: Form and Structure
topics.concept:
Every Present Perfect sentence has two parts: a helping verb (has or have) and the third form of the verb, called the past participle (V3).

Choose the helping verb by the subject:

  • Use has with third-person singular: he, she, it, and singular names (Ravi, the dog).
  • Use have with I, you, we, they, and plural subjects.

Negative and Question forms

FormPatternExample
AffirmativeS + has/have + V3She has eaten.
NegativeS + has/have + not + V3She has not (hasn't) eaten.
QuestionHas/Have + S + V3?Has she eaten?

The past participle (V3) is the part students forget. For regular verbs it ends in -ed (work → worked). For irregular verbs you must learn it: go → gone, write → written, eat → eaten, do → done.

examples.problem: Make this Present Perfect: I / write / the letter.
examples.solution:
I have written the letter.

Subject I takes have; the past participle of write is written (not 'wrote').

examples.problem: Make the negative of: He has completed the project.
examples.solution:
He has not (hasn't) completed the project.

Add not after the helping verb; the main verb stays as V3.

recap: has with he/she/it & singular; have with I/you/we/they & plural
Negative adds not after has/have; question puts has/have first
The trap is the past participle — learn irregular V3 forms

topics.title: When We Use the Present Perfect
topics.concept:
There are four classic situations. If a sentence fits one of them, the Present Perfect is usually right.

  1. An action just completed, with the result visible now: I have lost my keys. (so I can't get in)
  2. Life experience, when the time is not stated: She has visited Paris. (at some point in her life)
  3. An action that began in the past and continues now, with since/for: We have lived here for ten years.
  4. A repeated action up to now: He has called three times today.

The golden rule: if the sentence names an exact finished time (yesterday, in 2019, last week), use the Simple Past, not the Present Perfect.

examples.problem: Why is this correct: I have known her since 2018.?
examples.solution: The friendship started in the past and still continues — situation 3. Since 2018 marks the starting point, so the Present Perfect is right.

examples.problem: Choose: She ______ to London. (has gone / went) last summer.
examples.solution:
She went to London last summer.

'Last summer' is an exact finished time, so we use the Simple Past, not the Present Perfect.

recap: Use it for: just-completed action, life experience, action continuing now, repetition up to now
No exact past time is mentioned with the Present Perfect
If the time is finished and stated (yesterday, in 2019) → use Simple Past

topics.title: Time Markers: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for
topics.concept:
Certain signal words almost always travel with the Present Perfect. Learning them is the fastest way to pick the right tense in an exam.

MarkerMeaning & PositionExample
justa very short time ago (before V3)She has just left.
alreadysooner than expected (before V3)I have already eaten.
yetnegatives & questions (end)Have you finished yet?
everquestions: at any time (before V3)Have you ever flown?
nevernot at any time (before V3)I have never been late.
sincea point in time (start)since Monday, since 2020
fora length of timefor three hours, for years

since vs for is a favourite exam trap. Use since with a point (since 9 o'clock) and for with a duration (for two hours).

examples.solution: since — 2015 is a point in time, so we use since.

examples.problem: Fill in: We have waited ______ forty minutes.
examples.solution: for — forty minutes is a length of time, so we use for.

recap: just / already / never / ever go before the past participle
yet goes at the end of negatives and questions
since = a point in time; for = a length of time

questions.q: She ______ her homework.
questions.explanation: 'She' takes 'has' + past participle 'finished'.

questions.q: They ______ to Manali twice.
questions.explanation: Plural 'they' takes 'have' + 'been'.

questions.q: I have ______ this book before.
questions.explanation: The past participle of 'read' is 'read' (pronounced 'red').

questions.q: Choose the correct past participle of 'write'.
questions.explanation: write → wrote → written.

questions.q: We have lived here ______ five years.
questions.explanation: Five years is a duration, so use 'for'.

questions.q: He has known her ______ childhood.
questions.explanation: Childhood marks a starting point, so use 'since'.

questions.q: Which is the negative of 'She has eaten'?
questions.explanation: Add 'not' after the helping verb 'has'.

questions.q: ______ you ever visited Kerala?
questions.explanation: Subject 'you' takes 'Have' in a question.

questions.q: The marker 'yet' is normally placed:
questions.explanation: 'yet' goes at the end of negative and interrogative sentences.

questions.q: Identify the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'have' + past participle 'seen'.

questions.q: Pick the sentence that needs the Simple Past.
questions.explanation: 'an hour ago' is an exact finished time → Simple Past 'arrived'.

questions.q: Complete: 'It has ______ raining.' (start)
questions.explanation: After 'has', use the past participle 'started'.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: 'The students ______ their answers.'
questions.explanation: Plural 'students' takes 'have' + 'submitted'.

questions.q: Which word signals the Present Perfect?
questions.explanation: 'already' is a Present Perfect marker; the others are finished-time markers.

questions.q: Negative form: 'They have ______ seen snow.' (not at any time)
questions.explanation: 'never' means 'not at any time' and fits the Present Perfect.

questions.q: Fill in the blank with the correct option: 'Hardly had the bell rung when the students ______ out, an action that ______ every single day.'
questions.explanation: The narrative uses Simple Past 'rushed'; the habitual truth uses Simple Present 'happens'.

questions.q: Choose the option that correctly transforms: 'She started teaching here in 2015. She still teaches here.'
options: She has been teaching here since 2015.
questions.explanation: An action begun in the past and continuing uses the Present Perfect (Continuous) with 'since'.

questions.q: Identify the part with the error: 'The committee / have already / took / its decision.'
questions.explanation: After 'have already', the past participle 'taken' is required, not 'took'.

questions.q: Cloze: 'I have lived in three cities, but I ______ Mumbai the most.'
questions.explanation: An experience continuing to the present uses the Present Perfect 'have always loved'.

questions.q: Which sentence is free of error?
options: He has wrote a novel since two years.
He has written a novel for two years.
He is writing a novel since two years.
He wrote a novel for two years now.
questions.explanation: Correct participle 'written' and duration marker 'for' make option B correct.

questions.q: Rearrange into a correct question: 'long / how / have / you / known / him'
options: How long you have known him?
How long have you known him?
How have you long known him?
How long known have you him?
questions.explanation: Wh-word + auxiliary + subject + V3: 'How long have you known him?'

questions.q: Pick the correct tense: 'By the look of the wet road, it ______.'
questions.explanation: A just-finished action with a present result (wet road) takes the Present Perfect.

questions.q: Choose the sentence where the Present Perfect is WRONG.
options: She has gone to Delhi last Monday.
They have lived here for years.
questions.explanation: 'last Monday' is a finished time, so the Simple Past 'went' is needed.

questions.q: Fill in: 'Neither the captain nor the players ______ the trophy yet.'
questions.explanation: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject 'players' (plural) → 'have received'.

questions.q: Complete the editing task — the correct version of 'Since how long have you been waiting?' is:
options: Since how long are you waiting?
How long have you been waiting?
For how long you have waited?
questions.explanation: 'Since how long' is incorrect; the standard form is 'How long have you been waiting?'

outcomes: Form Present Perfect sentences correctly using has/have + past participle (V3)
Explain why we use the Present Perfect instead of the Simple Past
Use the markers just, already, yet, ever, never, since and for accurately
Spot and correct the most common Present Perfect mistakes
Answer MCQs and exam-pattern questions on this tense with confidence

intro.en: The Present Perfect connects the past to the present. We use it for an action that finished at an unstated time, but whose result still matters now. That is the whole idea in one line: the action is over, but its effect is alive in the present.
intro.hi: Present Perfect Tense भूतकाल को वर्तमान से जोड़ता है। इसका प्रयोग उन कार्यों के लिए होता है जो भूतकाल में पूरे हो चुके हैं, लेकिन जिनका प्रभाव अभी भी मौजूद है। एक पंक्ति में: काम खत्म हो गया, पर उसका असर अभी बाकी है।

real_life.situation:
You meet a friend outside the exam hall.

Friend: Have you finished the syllabus?

You: Yes, I have finished it.
real_life.why: The exact time you finished does not matter — what matters is that, right now, you are ready. The finishing happened in the past; the readiness is present. That link is exactly what the Present Perfect expresses.

common_mistakes.note: The past participle of go is gone, not went.
An exact past time (yesterday) needs the Simple Past.

common_mistakes.wrong: We have lived here since ten years.
common_mistakes.right: We have lived here for ten years.
common_mistakes.note: Use for with a length of time.

error_detection.correct: He has gone to the market.

rearrangement.answer: Have you ever been to Delhi?

reading.passage: Rohan has just completed Class 7. He has worked hard all year and has scored well in every test. He has already applied to the school debate club, and he has attended two practice sessions this week. He has never spoken in public before, but he has decided that this is the year he will try.

questions.q: What has Rohan just completed?
How many practice sessions has he attended this week?
questions.answer: He has attended two practice sessions.

questions.q: Find one sentence that shows a life experience (or lack of it).
questions.answer: "He has never spoken in public before." — it describes experience without a stated time.

speaking: She has just left for school.
We have lived in this city for five years.
Have you ever visited the Taj Mahal?
They have not finished the match yet.

writing.prompt: Write five sentences about things you have done today using the Present Perfect.
writing.example: I have brushed my teeth, I have eaten breakfast, and I have packed my bag.

micro_quiz.explanation: 'She' is third-person singular, so it takes 'has'.

micro_quiz.q: I have ______ my keys, so I can't open the door.

micro_quiz.explanation: 2020 is a point in time, so use 'since'.
'yet' is used at the end of questions and negatives.

challenge.q: Which sentence must use the Simple Past, NOT the Present Perfect?
challenge.explanation: 'in 2019' is an exact finished time, which requires the Simple Past: 'went'.

challenge.q: Identify the error: 'They has already ate their lunch.'
options: has should be have, ate should be eaten
challenge.explanation: Plural 'they' needs 'have', and the past participle of 'eat' is 'eaten'.
